phy_ocra.8.0.summary: Every magnet has two poles, a **north (north-seeking) pole** and a **south (south-seeking) pole**, where its magnetic effect is strongest. **Like poles repel and unlike poles attract**, and these forces are non-contact forces that get weaker as the magnets move apart. A **permanent magnet** produces its own magnetic field all the time, while an **induced magnet** is a magnetic material that only becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field, always attracts, and loses most or all of its magnetism when removed.

core.h: What a magnet is and where its poles are
core.p: A magnet is an object that produces its own **magnetic field**, a region around it where other magnets or magnetic materials feel a force. The magnetic effect is not spread evenly: it is concentrated at two ends called **poles**.
bullets: Every magnet has **two poles**: a **north pole** and a **south pole**. You can never get a magnet with just one pole.
The **north pole** is short for the **north-seeking pole**: if a bar magnet is hung so it can swing freely, this end turns to point towards the Earth's geographic north.
The **south pole** (south-seeking pole) points towards geographic south.
The magnetic field is **strongest at the poles**, which is why paper clips cluster at the ends of a bar magnet and hardly any stick to the middle.
If you cut a bar magnet in half you get **two smaller magnets**, each with its own north and south pole, not a separate N piece and S piece.

callouts.p: A place on a magnet where the magnetic forces are strongest. Every magnet has a north (north-seeking) pole and a south (south-seeking) pole.
Every magnet has both a north and a south pole. Cutting a magnet gives two complete magnets.

core.h: Forces between poles: like repel, unlike attract
core.p: When two magnets are brought close together, their poles exert forces on each other. The direction of the force depends only on which poles face each other.
bullets: **Like poles repel**: north and north push apart; south and south push apart.
**Unlike poles attract**: north and south pull together.
The forces always come in **equal and opposite pairs**: magnet A pushes or pulls magnet B exactly as hard as B pushes or pulls A (Newton's third law).
If you turn one magnet round, an attraction becomes a repulsion, because you have swapped which pole is facing the other magnet.
These forces can make a magnet move or turn, which is how a **compass needle** lines up with a field.

callouts.p: Like poles repel, unlike poles attract. Learn this exact wording: mark schemes reward it.
Write 'like poles repel', not 'like magnets repel'. Two magnets can attract or repel depending on which ends face each other.

core.h: Magnetism is a non-contact force
core.p: Magnetic forces act across a gap, even through air, paper or a vacuum. That makes magnetism a **non-contact force**, like gravity and the electrostatic force.
bullets: The magnets do not need to touch: the force is carried by the **magnetic field** around each magnet.
The force is **stronger when the magnets are closer** and **weaker when they are further apart**, because the field is strongest near the poles and spreads out with distance.
You can feel the force increase sharply as you push two repelling north poles towards each other.
Magnetic forces pass through non-magnetic materials such as paper, plastic, wood and glass, which is why a fridge magnet holds a sheet of paper in place.

callouts.p: Magnetic attraction is not the same as electrostatic (charge) attraction. A magnet does not attract a charged balloon because of its poles, and a rubbed rod does not have north and south poles.

core.h: Magnetic materials
core.p: Only a few materials are attracted to a magnet. These are called **magnetic materials**, and they are the only materials that can be made into magnets or have magnetism induced in them.
bullets: The common magnetic materials are **iron, steel, nickel and cobalt** (steel is mostly iron, so it is magnetic).
Most other metals are **not magnetic**: copper, aluminium, brass, gold, silver and lead are not attracted to a magnet.
Non-metals such as plastic, wood, glass and paper are not magnetic.
A magnetic material that is not a magnet is attracted to **either** pole of a magnet, north or south.
This is used to **sort scrap metal**: a large magnet lifts out iron and steel cans but leaves aluminium cans behind.

callouts.p: A very common wrong answer is 'all metals are magnetic'. Aluminium and copper are metals but are not attracted to a magnet.
If asked for magnetic materials, give iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.

core.h: Permanent magnets
core.p: A **permanent magnet** produces its **own magnetic field** all the time. It does not need another magnet nearby to be magnetic.
bullets: Examples: bar magnets, horseshoe magnets, fridge magnets, compass needles and the magnets inside loudspeakers and electric motors.
Permanent magnets are usually made from **steel** or special alloys, which keep their magnetism for a long time once magnetised.
A permanent magnet can **attract or repel** another magnet, depending on which poles face each other.
It can also attract magnetic materials such as iron and nickel by inducing magnetism in them.
Permanent magnets can lose their magnetism if they are heated strongly or hit repeatedly, so they should be stored carefully.

callouts.p: A magnet that produces its own magnetic field.

core.h: Induced magnets
core.p: An **induced magnet** is a piece of magnetic material that **becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field**. The magnetism is caused (induced) by the field of another magnet.
bullets: Hold an iron nail near a bar magnet and the nail itself becomes a magnet: it can then pick up a paper clip.
A chain of paper clips hanging from a magnet works because **each clip becomes an induced magnet** and attracts the next one.
The induced magnet has its own north and south poles while it is in the field.
When the induced magnet is **removed from the field** it **loses most or all of its magnetism quickly**: the paper clip chain falls apart when the top clip is pulled away from the magnet.
How long the induced magnetism lasts depends on the material: **soft iron** loses it almost at once, while **steel** keeps much of it (steel can be magnetised to make a permanent magnet).

callouts.p: A material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field. When removed from the field it loses most or all of its magnetism quickly.
The force between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet is always one of attraction.

core.h: Why induced magnetism always causes attraction
core.p: The poles of an induced magnet are set up by the magnet that induces them, and they always line up so that the **nearest induced pole is the opposite** of the pole that is close to it.
bullets: Bring the **north pole** of a magnet near an iron nail: the near end of the nail becomes a **south pole** and the far end a north pole.
Bring the **south pole** near instead: the near end of the nail becomes a **north pole**.
Either way, **unlike poles face each other**, so the force is always **attraction**.
This is why a magnetic material is attracted to both ends of a magnet and can never be repelled by one.
It is also why attraction alone cannot prove that an object is a permanent magnet.

callouts.p: An induced magnet always has the opposite pole nearest the inducing magnet's pole, so it is always attracted.

core.h: Comparing permanent and induced magnets
core.p: The spec asks you to **describe the difference** between permanent and induced magnets. A full answer compares where the field comes from, what forces can occur and what happens when the other magnet is taken away.
bullets: Source of field: a permanent magnet makes **its own** field; an induced magnet is only magnetic because it is **in another magnet's field**.
Forces: a permanent magnet can **attract or repel** another magnet; an induced magnet is **only ever attracted**.
When removed: a permanent magnet **stays magnetic**; an induced magnet **loses most or all** of its magnetism quickly.
Poles: a permanent magnet's poles are fixed; an induced magnet's poles depend on which pole of the inducing magnet is near it.

callouts.p: In a 'describe the difference' question, say what each type does. 'An induced magnet loses its magnetism' scores more fully if you add 'but a permanent magnet keeps its magnetism'.

core.h: Testing whether an object is a permanent magnet
core.p: Because induced magnetism always attracts, the only reliable test for a permanent magnet is **repulsion**.
bullets: Bring each end of the unknown object in turn up to **one pole** of a known magnet.
If **one end is repelled**, the object must be a permanent magnet, because only two magnets with like poles facing can repel.
If **both ends are attracted**, the object is a magnetic material (it is an unmagnetised piece, magnetised by induction).
If there is **no force** at all, the object is not a magnetic material (for example copper or aluminium).
Attraction proves nothing on its own: it happens with permanent magnets (unlike poles) and with magnetic materials (induced magnetism).

callouts.p: Repulsion is the only sure test for a magnet.
'It was attracted so it is a magnet' is wrong: an iron bar is attracted but is not necessarily a magnet.

core.h: Soft iron and steel: choosing a material
core.p: Different magnetic materials behave differently as induced magnets, and this decides what they are used for.
bullets: **Soft iron** is magnetised easily in a field and **loses its magnetism almost immediately** when the field is removed. This makes it ideal for things that must switch on and off, such as the **core of an electromagnet** or a scrapyard crane.
**Steel** is harder to magnetise but **keeps its magnetism** after the field is removed, so it is used to make **permanent magnets** such as compass needles and fridge magnets.
A steel paper clip left on a magnet for a long time can stay slightly magnetised and pick up another clip afterwards.
Choosing the wrong one causes problems: a steel electromagnet core would stay magnetic after the current is switched off, so the crane could not drop its load.

callouts.p: For 2 marks, state the property (loses magnetism quickly) and link it to the use (so the electromagnet can be switched off).

core.h: Everyday uses of poles and induced magnetism
core.p: Many devices rely on the simple rules of attraction, repulsion and induction.
bullets: **Fridge door seals** contain a flexible permanent magnet that is attracted to the steel door frame by induction, sealing the door.
**Magnetic catches** on cupboards hold a steel plate by induced attraction.
**Compasses** use a small permanent magnet that turns because its poles are attracted and repelled by the Earth's magnetic field.
**Scrap metal sorting** separates iron and steel (attracted) from aluminium (not attracted).
**Maglev trains** and some toys use repulsion between like poles to push objects apart without contact.

callouts.p: A fridge magnet sticks to the door because the steel door becomes an induced magnet with the opposite pole nearest, so they attract.

analogy.p: Think of poles as dancers who only want partners of the other type: an N dancer is drawn to an S dancer (unlike attract) and pushes away another N (like repel). A permanent magnet is a dancer who always knows their role. An induced magnet is a beginner who copies whoever approaches: if an N dancer comes near, the beginner turns their S side to face them, so they always end up attracted. When the confident dancer leaves, a soft iron beginner forgets the routine at once, while a steel beginner remembers it. Where it breaks down: real magnetic forces need no 'wanting', they act through a field across empty space, the force grows smoothly stronger as distance shrinks, and the forces on the two magnets are always equal and opposite.

terms.d: An object that produces its own magnetic field.
The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.
A place on a magnet where the magnetic forces are strongest.
The north-seeking pole: the end of a freely suspended magnet that points towards geographic north.
The south-seeking pole: the end of a freely suspended magnet that points towards geographic south.
Two poles of the same type (N and N, or S and S); they repel.
A north pole and a south pole; they attract.
A force that pulls two objects towards each other.
A force that pushes two objects apart.
A force that acts between objects that are not touching, such as the magnetic force.
A material that is attracted to a magnet and can be magnetised: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field all the time.
A material that becomes a magnet when placed in a magnetic field and loses most or all of its magnetism quickly when removed.
Magnetism caused in a magnetic material by the field of another magnet; it always causes attraction.
A magnetic material that is easily magnetised and loses its magnetism almost immediately; used for electromagnet cores.
A magnetic material, mainly iron, that keeps its magnetism once magnetised; used for permanent magnets.

mistakes.w: Like magnets repel and unlike magnets attract.
mistakes.r: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

mistakes.w: All metals are attracted to magnets.
mistakes.r: Only magnetic materials such as iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are attracted; copper and aluminium are not.

mistakes.w: The object was attracted to the magnet so it must be a magnet.
mistakes.r: Attraction also happens with unmagnetised magnetic materials; only repulsion proves an object is a permanent magnet.

mistakes.w: An induced magnet can be repelled if you use the other pole.
mistakes.r: Induced magnetism always causes attraction because the opposite pole is induced nearest the magnet.

mistakes.w: An induced magnet stays magnetic after it is removed from the field.
mistakes.r: An induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly when removed from the field.

mistakes.w: A permanent magnet only produces a field when another magnet is near.
mistakes.r: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field all the time.

mistakes.w: Cutting a bar magnet in half gives a north piece and a south piece.
mistakes.r: Each half becomes a complete magnet with its own north and south pole.

mistakes.w: Steel is used for electromagnet cores because it is strongly magnetic.
mistakes.r: Soft iron is used because it loses its magnetism quickly when the current is switched off; steel would stay magnetised.

mistakes.w: Magnetic forces get stronger further from the magnet.
mistakes.r: Magnetic forces are strongest at the poles and get weaker as distance increases.

exam.q: State what happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought close to the north pole of another magnet.
model: They repel (push apart).
exam.tip: Use 'repel', the exact mark-scheme word.

exam.q: Name two magnetic materials.
model: Any two from: iron, steel, nickel, cobalt (1 mark each).
exam.tip: Do not give 'metal' or 'copper'.

exam.q: Which of these is a magnetic material: aluminium, copper, nickel, brass?
model: Nickel.
exam.tip: Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are the common magnetic materials.

exam.q: State the difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet.
model: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field.
An induced magnet only becomes a magnet when placed in a magnetic field (and loses its magnetism when removed).
exam.tip: Describe both types, not just one.

exam.q: A student says a paper clip is attracted to both the north and south poles of a bar magnet. Explain why.
model: The paper clip becomes an induced magnet.
The pole induced nearest the magnet is always the opposite pole, so it is always attracted.
exam.tip: The key word is 'induced'.

exam.q: Describe what happens to a chain of iron paper clips hanging from a magnet when the top clip is pulled away from the magnet. Explain your answer.
model: The clips fall apart / no longer hold together.
They were induced magnets and lose (most or all of) their magnetism when removed from the magnetic field.
exam.tip: Give the observation and the reason.

exam.q: Explain why soft iron, not steel, is used for the core of an electromagnet in a scrapyard crane.
model: Soft iron loses its magnetism (almost) immediately when the current is switched off.
So the crane can release the scrap; steel would stay magnetised.
exam.tip: Link the property to the job the crane has to do.

exam.q: Explain how a fridge magnet holds onto a steel fridge door.
model: Magnetism is induced in the steel door.
The opposite pole is induced nearest the magnet, so there is attraction.
exam.tip: Mention that the door becomes an induced magnet.

exam.q: Two bar magnets are placed end to end. Magnet A is labelled N on the left and S on the right. Magnet B is to its right, labelled S on the left and N on the right. State and explain the force between them.
model: Repulsion.
The south pole of A faces the south pole of B, and like poles repel.
exam.tip: Work out which two poles face each other first.

exam.q: A student has three identical-looking metal bars, X, Y and Z, and a bar magnet. Describe how the student could find out which bar is a permanent magnet, which is an unmagnetised magnetic material and which is non-magnetic.
model: Bring one pole of the bar magnet near each end of each bar in turn.
A bar where one end is repelled is a permanent magnet.
Because repulsion only happens between like poles of two magnets.
A bar where both ends are attracted is an unmagnetised magnetic material.
Because magnetism is induced in it, and induced magnetism always causes attraction.
A bar with no force on either end is non-magnetic (e.g. aluminium or copper).
Attraction alone cannot identify a permanent magnet, so both ends must be tested.
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need method, results and reasons in a logical order.

exam.q: Describe the differences between permanent and induced magnets. Include an example of each and explain why the force between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet is always attractive.
model: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field, e.g. a bar magnet or compass needle.
An induced magnet becomes a magnet only when placed in a magnetic field, e.g. an iron nail near a magnet.
A permanent magnet keeps its magnetism; an induced magnet loses most or all of it quickly when removed from the field.
A permanent magnet can attract or repel another magnet.
The pole induced nearest the permanent magnet is always the opposite (unlike) pole.
Unlike poles attract, so the force is always attraction.
exam.tip: Cover source of field, behaviour when removed, possible forces and the reason for attraction.

worked.q: Magnet P is arranged N then S from left to right. Magnet Q is to its right, arranged N then S. Then Q is turned round. What is the force between them before and after Q is turned?
steps: Before: the right end of P is S and the left end of Q is N.
S facing N are unlike poles, so they attract.
After turning Q round, its left end is now S.
S of P faces S of Q: like poles, so they repel.
worked.ans: Before: attraction. After turning Q round: repulsion.

worked.q: An unknown rod is tested with the north pole of a bar magnet. End 1 is attracted. End 2 is also attracted. A student concludes the rod is a magnet. Evaluate this conclusion.
steps: If the rod were a permanent magnet, one of its ends would be a north pole.
That north end would be repelled by the north pole of the bar magnet.
Neither end was repelled, so the rod is not a permanent magnet.
Both ends were attracted because magnetism was induced in the rod, with a south pole induced nearest the magnet each time.
So the rod is an unmagnetised magnetic material such as iron, steel, nickel or cobalt.
worked.ans: The conclusion is wrong: the rod is a magnetic material, not a permanent magnet, because only repulsion proves magnetism.

worked.q: An iron nail is touched against the south pole of a bar magnet. Which pole is induced at the end of the nail touching the magnet, and at the far end? What happens when the nail is pulled off?
steps: The induced pole nearest the inducing pole is always the opposite pole.
The magnet's south pole touches the nail, so a north pole is induced at the touching end.
The far end of the nail becomes a south pole.
Iron is a soft magnetic material, so when the nail is removed from the field it loses most or all of its magnetism quickly.
worked.ans: North pole at the touching end, south pole at the far end; the nail loses most or all of its magnetism when pulled away.

phy_ocra.8.1.summary: A **magnetic field** is the region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or a magnetic material, and we show it with **magnetic field lines** that point from **north to south**. The **direction** of the field at any point is the way the north pole of a compass points, and the **strength** is shown by how **close together** the lines are, so the field of a bar magnet is strongest at the poles and weakens with distance. A freely turning **compass** always lines up north-south even far from any magnet, which is evidence that the **Earth has its own magnetic field** produced by a magnetic core, behaving like a giant bar magnet with its magnetic south pole near the geographic North Pole.

core.h: What a magnetic field is
core.p: A **magnetic field** is the region around a magnet where a **force** acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt). The force is non-contact, so the field is how the magnet 'reaches out' across space.
bullets: Every magnet is surrounded by a magnetic field; it is invisible but its effects can be detected.
The field has both a **strength** and a **direction** at every point, and both **change from one point to another**.
We detect the field with a **plotting compass** (shows direction) or **iron filings** (show the pattern).
The force on a magnetic object is bigger where the field is **stronger**.

callouts.p: The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.

core.h: Magnetic field lines
core.p: Field lines (also called lines of force) are a model for showing the shape, direction and strength of a magnetic field.
bullets: Field lines always point **from the north pole to the south pole** outside a magnet.
The **direction** of the field at a point is the direction the **north pole of a plotting compass** points when placed there.
Every line must carry an **arrow** showing direction: unarrowed lines lose marks.
Field lines **never cross**: the field can only have one direction at each point.
The **closer together** the lines, the **stronger** the field; lines spreading out show the field getting weaker.
Lines start and finish on the magnet (they leave the N pole and enter the S pole); they do not stop in mid-air.

callouts.p: Direction: north to south, the way a compass north pole points. Strength: shown by how close the field lines are.
Drawing field lines that cross or touch is a common error and is always marked wrong.

core.h: The field around a bar magnet
core.p: The field pattern of a single bar magnet is the one you must be able to draw from memory.
bullets: Lines come **out of the north pole**, curve round the outside and go **into the south pole**.
The lines are **most concentrated at the poles**, so the field is **strongest at the poles**.
Further from the magnet the lines **spread out**, so the field gets **weaker with distance**.
The pattern is **symmetrical** above and below the magnet.
Along the sides near the middle of the magnet the field is weak, which is why few paper clips stick there.
The direction changes from point to point: near the N pole it points away, near the S pole it points towards, and alongside the magnet it runs parallel to it from N towards S.

callouts.p: At least four or five lines, arrows N to S on every line, lines closest at the poles, no lines crossing, lines touching the magnet at the ends.

core.h: Fields between two magnets
core.p: When two magnets are close together their fields combine to make a new pattern.
bullets: **Unlike poles facing (N to S)**: lines run straight across the gap from N to S; magnets **attract**.
Between flat, opposite poles close together the lines are **parallel and equally spaced**: this is a **uniform field**, the same strength and direction everywhere in the gap.
**Like poles facing (N to N or S to S)**: lines from each magnet push away from each other and bend aside; magnets **repel**.
Between two like poles there is a **neutral point** in the middle where the two fields cancel and a compass does not settle in any particular direction.
A uniform field is used in experiments on the motor effect because the force on a wire is then the same everywhere in the gap.

head: Arrangement
Field pattern in gap
Force
rows: Lines straight across, N to S
Flat N and S poles close together

callouts.p: A field with the same strength and direction at every point, shown by parallel, equally spaced field lines.

core.h: Practical: plotting a field with compasses
core.p: A **plotting compass** is a small compass whose needle is a tiny magnet. It lines up with the field at the point where it is placed, so it can be used to trace field lines.
bullets: Place the bar magnet on a sheet of paper and draw round it.
Put the plotting compass near the **north pole** and mark a dot at the end the compass needle **points to**.
Move the compass so its tail is on the dot you just made and mark a new dot at its tip.
Repeat until you reach the south pole, then join the dots with a smooth curve and add an arrow **N to S**.
Repeat starting from different points around the N pole to build up the whole pattern.
**Advantage**: shows the **direction** of the field. **Limitation**: slow, and the compass has a size so positions are approximate.

callouts.p: The north-seeking (usually red or arrowed) end of the needle shows the field direction.

core.h: Practical: showing a field with iron filings
core.p: Sprinkling **iron filings** on paper over a magnet gives a fast picture of the whole field pattern.
bullets: Place a sheet of paper or card over the magnet and sprinkle iron filings thinly on top.
Tap the paper gently so the filings can move.
Each filing becomes a tiny **induced magnet** and lines up along the field, forming the pattern of field lines.
The filings crowd together where the field is **strongest** (at the poles).
**Advantage**: shows the whole **shape** quickly. **Limitation**: does **not show direction**, so you cannot add arrows without a compass.
Safety: avoid getting filings in the eyes and keep them off the magnet itself (use paper).

callouts.p: Iron filings show the pattern but not which way the field points; you need a compass for direction.

core.h: How field strength and direction change from point to point
core.p: The spec asks you to describe how both **strength** and **direction** vary around a magnet, not just to draw the pattern.
bullets: **Strength** is greatest at the poles, where the lines are closest; it **decreases with distance** from the magnet as the lines spread out.
Two points at the same distance from a pole but on different sides can have the **same strength but different directions**.
**Direction** at any point is along the **tangent** to the field line there, in the direction of the arrow.
A compass moved around a bar magnet turns gradually, showing the direction changing smoothly.
Far from any magnet, the bar magnet's field becomes too weak to notice and a compass just points along the Earth's field.

callouts.p: The further from the magnet, the more spread out the field lines and the weaker the field.

core.h: How a compass works
core.p: A **compass** contains a small **permanent magnet** (the needle) that is free to turn.
bullets: The needle feels forces from any magnetic field it is in, which turn it until it lines up **along the field**.
Its north-seeking pole points in the **direction of the field** at that point.
Near a bar magnet, the compass lines up with the magnet's field, which is much stronger close up.
Away from any magnet, a compass still settles pointing **north-south**: something must be producing a magnetic field everywhere on Earth.
Because the needle is a permanent magnet, its north pole is attracted to a magnetic south pole and repelled by a magnetic north pole.

callouts.p: A small magnet, free to rotate, that lines up with the magnetic field; its north pole points in the direction of the field.

core.h: Evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic
core.p: The behaviour of a compass gives the evidence that the **Earth has a magnetic field** that comes from its **core**.
bullets: A compass points **north-south** at any place on Earth, even far from any magnet, so there must be a **magnetic field everywhere** around the Earth.
The pattern of directions measured all over the Earth matches the field of a **giant bar magnet** inside it.
A field this large, reaching right across the planet and out into space, must come from **inside the Earth**: the **core** must be magnetic.
The core is mainly **iron (and nickel)**, which are magnetic materials, supporting this idea.
At different places a compass that can tilt also dips into the ground, just as it would near the pole of a bar magnet, giving further evidence of the bar-magnet-like shape.

callouts.p: A freely suspended magnet always lines up north-south, so the Earth must have a magnetic field, so its core must be magnetic.
Observation (compass points N-S everywhere), deduction (there is a magnetic field), conclusion (it must come from a magnetic core).

core.h: The Earth's magnetic field and its poles
core.p: The Earth's field is shaped like the field of a bar magnet, but the naming of the poles catches many students out.
bullets: A compass's **north pole** points to the **geographic North Pole**.
Since **unlike poles attract**, there must be a **magnetic south pole** near the geographic North Pole.
So the Earth behaves as if it has a bar magnet inside with its **south pole under the Arctic** and its **north pole under the Antarctic**.
Field lines outside the Earth go **from the southern hemisphere to the northern hemisphere** (from the magnetic north pole to the magnetic south pole).
The magnetic poles are **close to**, but not exactly at, the geographic poles.

callouts.p: The geographic North Pole is a magnetic south pole. That is why the north pole of a compass is attracted to it.

analogy.t: Field lines as traffic on a one-way road map
analogy.p: Picture field lines as one-way roads leaving a city called N and arriving at a city called S. Arrows show the one-way direction, roads never cross (no junctions allowed), and near each city the roads are packed tightly together like busy streets, which means a strong field. Out in the countryside the roads spread out, so the field is weak. A compass is a car that can only drive along these roads in the direction of the arrows. Where it breaks down: nothing actually travels along a field line, the lines are only a model, and the field exists everywhere between the lines too, not just on them.

terms.d: The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or magnetic material.
A line showing the direction of the force on a north pole; drawn from north to south with arrows.
The direction the north pole of a plotting compass points at that point.
How strong the magnetic field is at a point, shown by how close together the field lines are.
A field with the same strength and direction everywhere, shown by parallel, equally spaced lines.
A point where two magnetic fields cancel out, so there is no overall field.
A small compass used to find the direction of a magnetic field at a point.
Small pieces of iron that become induced magnets and line up with a field to show its pattern.
A small, freely turning permanent magnet that lines up with a magnetic field.
The magnetic field around the Earth, produced by its magnetic core, shaped like the field of a bar magnet.
The centre of the Earth, made mainly of iron and nickel; the source of the Earth's magnetic field.
The northern end of the Earth's axis of rotation; a magnetic south pole lies close to it.
The pole of the Earth's magnetic field near the geographic North Pole, which attracts the north pole of a compass.
A line that just touches a curve at one point; the field direction is along the tangent to the field line.

mistakes.w: Field lines go from south to north.
mistakes.r: Field lines go from north to south outside a magnet.

mistakes.w: Drawing field lines with no arrows.
mistakes.r: Every field line needs an arrow pointing from N to S.

mistakes.w: Drawing field lines that cross.
mistakes.r: Field lines never cross, because the field has only one direction at each point.

mistakes.w: The field is strongest in the middle of the magnet.
mistakes.r: The field is strongest at the poles, where the field lines are closest together.

mistakes.w: Iron filings show the direction of the field.
mistakes.r: Iron filings only show the pattern; a plotting compass is needed to show the direction.

mistakes.w: The geographic North Pole is a magnetic north pole.
mistakes.r: There is a magnetic south pole near the geographic North Pole, which is why it attracts a compass's north pole.

mistakes.w: A compass points north because the North Pole is cold or made of iron.
mistakes.r: A compass lines up with the Earth's magnetic field, which is produced by the Earth's magnetic core.

mistakes.w: Wider spaced lines mean a stronger field.
mistakes.r: Closer lines mean a stronger field; spreading lines mean the field is weaker.

exam.q: State the direction of magnetic field lines around a bar magnet.
model: From the north pole to the south pole.
exam.tip: Say 'north to south', not just 'round the magnet'.

exam.q: Where is the magnetic field of a bar magnet strongest?
model: At the poles.
exam.tip: Link it to the field lines being closest there.

exam.q: How does a field line diagram show where the magnetic field is strongest?
model: Where the field lines are closest together.
exam.tip: Use 'closest together' or 'most concentrated'.

exam.q: Draw the magnetic field pattern around a bar magnet.
model: Lines leaving the N pole and entering the S pole (curved, symmetrical).
Arrows on lines pointing from N to S.
Lines closer together at the poles and no lines crossing.
exam.tip: Arrows and spacing are where marks are most often lost.

exam.q: Describe how a plotting compass can be used to plot the field lines of a bar magnet.
model: Place the magnet on paper and put the compass near the N pole.
Mark the position the compass needle points to with a dot.
Move the compass so its tail is at the dot and mark again; repeat until the S pole.
Join the dots with a smooth line and add an arrow from N to S; repeat from other starting points.
exam.tip: Step by step, in order, with the arrow at the end.

exam.q: Give one advantage of using iron filings instead of a plotting compass to show a magnetic field, and one disadvantage.
model: Advantage: shows the whole pattern quickly.
Disadvantage: does not show the direction of the field.
exam.tip: Direction is the key thing filings cannot show.

exam.q: Describe the field between a flat north pole and a flat south pole placed close together.
model: Field lines are parallel and equally spaced, from N to S.
The field is uniform: the same strength and direction everywhere in the gap.
exam.tip: 'Uniform' is the word the mark scheme wants.

exam.q: A compass is placed on a table far away from any magnets. Explain why it points north-south.
model: The compass needle is a magnet that lines up with a magnetic field.
The Earth has a magnetic field (produced by its core), so the needle lines up with the Earth's field.
exam.tip: Mention the Earth's field, not just 'it points to the North Pole'.

exam.q: Explain why the magnetic pole near the Earth's geographic North Pole is a magnetic south pole.
model: The north pole of a compass is attracted towards the geographic North Pole.
Unlike poles attract, so it must be a magnetic south pole.
exam.tip: Use the 'unlike poles attract' rule as your reason.

exam.q: Explain how the behaviour of magnetic compasses provides evidence that the core of the Earth is magnetic. Describe the shape of the Earth's magnetic field in your answer.
model: A freely suspended compass always settles pointing north-south, wherever it is on the Earth.
So there must be a magnetic field everywhere around the Earth.
The directions of compasses at different places match the field pattern of a bar magnet.
The field is so large it must come from inside the Earth: the core must be magnetic (it contains iron and nickel).
The Earth's field is like that of a bar magnet with its south pole near the geographic North Pole.
Field lines leave the southern hemisphere and go round the outside of the Earth into the northern hemisphere.
exam.tip: Observation, then deduction, then conclusion, then the field shape with correct pole names.

worked.q: A plotting compass is placed at four points: A just beyond the N pole of a bar magnet, B just beyond the S pole, C beside the middle of the magnet and D far from the magnet. Describe which way the compass points at each and where the field is strongest.
steps: The compass north pole points along the field line, which goes from N to S.
At A the field points away from the N pole, so the compass points away from the magnet.
At B the field points into the S pole, so the compass points towards the magnet.
At C the field runs alongside the magnet from the N end towards the S end, so the compass points parallel to the magnet, towards S.
At D the bar magnet's field is too weak to notice, so the compass lines up with the Earth's field and points north.
The field is strongest at A and B (the poles), where the field lines are closest together.
worked.ans: A: away from magnet; B: towards magnet; C: parallel to magnet pointing N to S; D: north (Earth's field). Strongest at A and B.

worked.q: Model answer: a student says 'the Earth's magnetic north pole is at the North Pole, because compasses point there'. Correct the statement.
steps: The end of a compass that points north is its north pole.
The north pole of the compass is attracted to the geographic North Pole.
Unlike poles attract, so the magnetic pole near the geographic North Pole must be a south pole.
So the Earth acts like a bar magnet with its south pole in the Arctic and its north pole in the Antarctic.
worked.ans: The pole near the geographic North Pole is a magnetic south pole; compass north poles point to it because unlike poles attract.

phy_ocra.8.2.summary: An **electric current** flowing through a wire produces a **magnetic field** around it, which can be shown by the deflection of a compass placed near the wire. Around a long straight wire the field lines are **concentric circles**, with a direction given by the **right-hand grip rule**, and the field is **stronger for a larger current** and **weaker further from the wire**. Coiling the wire into a **solenoid** concentrates the field, making it **strong and uniform inside** and shaped like a **bar magnet's field outside**, and adding an **iron core** makes an even stronger **electromagnet** that can be switched on and off.

core.h: Showing that a current has a magnetic effect
core.p: Any wire carrying an electric current is surrounded by a **magnetic field**. This is called the **magnetic effect of a current**, and it is easy to demonstrate with a compass.
bullets: Place a **plotting compass** next to a straight wire connected to a d.c. supply, with the switch open: the compass points north (Earth's field).
Close the switch so a current flows: the compass needle **deflects**, showing a magnetic field around the wire.
**Reverse the current** (swap the supply connections): the needle deflects the **opposite way**, so the field direction has reversed.
**Switch off** the current: the needle returns to pointing north, so the field only exists **while current flows**.
**Increase the current**: the deflection is larger, showing a stronger field.
Use a large current for a short time only, because the wire can get hot.

callouts.p: A current flowing through a conductor produces a magnetic field around the conductor.
For full marks, say what you would observe (compass needle deflects) and what changes when the current is reversed or switched off.

core.h: Field pattern around a straight wire
core.p: The field around a long straight wire is not like a bar magnet's: there are no poles. The field lines form **concentric circles** around the wire.
bullets: The field lines are **circles centred on the wire**, in planes at **right angles** to the wire.
The circles are **closer together near the wire** and **further apart further away**, showing the field gets weaker with distance.
Every circle needs an arrow; all circles around one wire go the **same way round**.
The pattern can be shown with iron filings sprinkled on a horizontal card with the wire passing vertically through it, and the direction found with plotting compasses placed on the card.
Reversing the current **reverses the direction** of every field line but keeps the same circular pattern.

callouts.p: Circles that share the same centre; around a straight wire the centre is the wire itself.
Draw the circles getting further apart as you move away from the wire. Equally spaced circles suggest the field is the same strength everywhere, which is wrong.

core.h: The right-hand grip rule
core.p: The **right-hand grip rule** tells you which way the field lines go round a wire.
bullets: Imagine gripping the wire with your **right hand**, with your **thumb pointing in the direction of the (conventional) current**.
Your **fingers curl round** in the **direction of the magnetic field**.
Conventional current flows from **positive to negative** around the circuit.
In end-on diagrams, a **dot** means current coming **out of the page** (towards you) and a **cross** means current going **into the page** (away from you).
Current **out of the page** (dot): field lines go **anticlockwise**. Current **into the page** (cross): field lines go **clockwise**.

callouts.p: Right hand only. Thumb along the current, curled fingers show the field direction.
Think of an arrow: you see the point (dot) when it comes towards you and the tail feathers (cross) when it goes away.

core.h: What affects the strength of the field around a wire
core.p: The spec says you must recall that the strength of the field depends on the **current** and the **distance from the wire**.
bullets: **Larger current**: **stronger** magnetic field; the field lines are drawn closer together.
**Greater distance** from the wire: **weaker** magnetic field; the circles are further apart.
Doubling the current doubles the strength of the field at a given point.
Close to the wire the field can be strong enough to deflect a compass noticeably; a short distance away the effect becomes very small.
Reversing the current changes the **direction** of the field but **not its strength**.

callouts.p: Field strength increases with current and decreases with distance from the wire.

core.h: Solenoids
core.p: A **solenoid** is a long coil of wire. Wrapping the wire into a coil makes the fields from each turn **add together**, so the field is much stronger than for a single straight wire.
bullets: Inside the solenoid the fields from each turn line up in the **same direction** and reinforce each other.
Inside, the field is **strong and uniform**: field lines are **parallel and equally spaced**.
Outside, the field is the **same shape as a bar magnet's field**, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.
Outside the solenoid the fields from opposite sides of the coil partly cancel, so the field there is **weak**.
The field lines form complete loops: out of the N end, round the outside, into the S end, and back through the inside from S to N.

callouts.p: A long coil of wire. When a current flows it produces a magnetic field like that of a bar magnet, strong and uniform inside the coil.
Outside, field lines go N to S as usual, but inside the coil they run from the S end to the N end to complete the loops.

core.h: Finding the poles of a solenoid
core.p: Which end is north depends on the **direction of the current** in the coil, and it can be worked out in two ways.
bullets: **Right-hand grip rule for a coil**: curl the fingers of your right hand round the coil in the **direction of the current**; your **thumb points to the north pole**.
**End-view method**: look at one end of the coil. If the current flows **anticlockwise**, that end is a **north pole**; if **clockwise**, it is a **south pole**.
Memory aid: draw an N with arrows on its ends (anticlockwise) and an S with arrows (clockwise).
**Reversing the current** swaps the poles: the N end becomes S and vice versa.
Check with a plotting compass: its north pole points away from the N end of the solenoid.

callouts.p: For a coil, the right-hand grip rule swaps roles: fingers follow the current round the turns, thumb shows north and the field direction inside.

core.h: Making a solenoid's field stronger
core.p: The spec asks how the solenoid arrangement **enhances** the magnetic effect. There are three ways to make the field stronger.
bullets: **Increase the current** through the coil.
**Increase the number of turns** (more turns on the same length), so more fields add together.
**Put an iron core** inside the coil: the iron becomes an **induced magnet** whose field adds to the solenoid's, making the field **much stronger**.
Making the coil **longer** with the same number of turns spreads them out and does **not** help; it is turns per length that matters.
These factors are why electromagnets for lifting scrap use large currents, many turns and an iron core.

callouts.p: A solenoid's field is made stronger by increasing the current, increasing the number of turns and adding an iron core.

core.h: Electromagnets
core.p: An **electromagnet** is a solenoid with a **soft iron core**. It is a magnet that can be **switched on and off** and whose strength can be changed.
bullets: When current flows, the solenoid's field magnetises the iron core, giving a strong magnet.
When the current is switched off, **soft iron loses its magnetism almost immediately**, so the electromagnet stops attracting.
A **steel** core would stay magnetised and so would not switch off properly.
The strength can be **controlled** by changing the current.
Uses include **scrapyard cranes**, **relays**, **electric bells**, door locks and circuit breakers.

callouts.p: A solenoid with an iron core that becomes a magnet when a current flows through it.

core.h: Comparing the fields of a wire, a solenoid and a bar magnet
core.p: Comparing the three patterns helps you choose the right picture in an exam.
bullets: **Straight wire**: concentric circles, no poles, weaker further away.
**Solenoid**: uniform inside; bar-magnet shape outside, with N and S poles at the ends.
**Bar magnet**: lines from N to S outside, strongest at the poles.
A solenoid behaves like a bar magnet: its ends attract and repel the poles of other magnets in the same way.

core.h: Why coiling the wire concentrates the field
core.p: Grade 9 answers explain the solenoid in terms of the fields of the individual turns.
bullets: Each turn of the coil behaves like a short piece of wire with circular field lines round it.
Inside the coil, the field from every part of every turn points the **same way along the axis**, so the fields **add** (reinforce).
Outside, the field from the top of a turn and the bottom of that turn point in roughly **opposite directions**, so they partly **cancel**.
So the field is concentrated inside, giving a **strong, uniform** field there, and weaker outside.
More turns means more contributions adding together inside, which is why more turns give a stronger field.

callouts.p: In 'explain why the field inside is strong' questions, say the fields from each turn reinforce (add together) inside the coil.

analogy.p: A straight current-carrying wire is like a straw spinning in a bath: the water swirls round it in circles, fast close to the straw and slower further away, like the field getting weaker with distance. Spin the straw the other way (reverse the current) and the swirl reverses. A solenoid is like lining up many spinning straws in a ring: their swirls all push water the same way through the middle, producing a strong, steady flow along the inside, like the uniform field in a coil. Where it breaks down: nothing actually flows round a wire, the magnetic field is not a moving substance, and the field also exists in a vacuum where there is no water at all.

terms.d: The magnetic field produced around a conductor when a current flows through it.
The direction of current from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a supply.
Circles with the same centre; the field pattern around a straight current-carrying wire.
Grip the wire with the right hand, thumb along the current: the fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic field.
Shows current flowing out of the page, towards the viewer.
Shows current flowing into the page, away from the viewer.
A long coil of wire that produces a magnetic field like a bar magnet when a current flows.
A field with the same strength and direction everywhere, as inside a solenoid.
A solenoid with a soft iron core that is magnetic only while current flows.
A piece of iron inside a solenoid that is magnetised by induction, making the field much stronger, and loses its magnetism when the current stops.
The individual loops of wire in a coil; more turns give a stronger field.
A small compass used to show the direction of a magnetic field at a point.
A switch operated by an electromagnet, so a small current can switch a larger current on or off.
How strong a magnetic field is at a point; shown by how close the field lines are.

mistakes.w: The field around a straight wire has a north pole and a south pole.
mistakes.r: The field around a straight wire is concentric circles with no poles.

mistakes.w: Drawing the circles round a wire equally spaced.
mistakes.r: The circles should get further apart further from the wire, because the field gets weaker.

mistakes.w: Using the left hand to find the direction of the field round a wire.
mistakes.r: Use the right-hand grip rule: thumb along the current, fingers show the field.

mistakes.w: Making a solenoid longer makes the field stronger.
mistakes.r: Increasing the number of turns (on the same length), the current or adding an iron core makes the field stronger.

mistakes.w: Steel is used for the core of an electromagnet.
mistakes.r: Soft iron is used because it loses its magnetism quickly when the current is switched off.

mistakes.w: The field inside a solenoid is weak.
mistakes.r: The field inside a solenoid is strong and uniform; outside it is weaker and shaped like a bar magnet's field.

mistakes.w: Reversing the current makes the field weaker.
mistakes.r: Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field; the strength is unchanged.

mistakes.w: The magnetic field stays after the current is switched off.
mistakes.r: The field only exists while the current flows.

exam.q: State what happens to a compass needle placed next to a wire when a current is switched on in the wire.
model: It deflects / moves / changes direction.
exam.tip: Then say why: the current produces a magnetic field.

exam.q: Describe the shape of the magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire.
model: Concentric circles around the wire.
Getting further apart further from the wire.
exam.tip: Both the shape and the spacing earn marks.

exam.q: State two factors that affect the strength of the magnetic field around a straight wire.
model: The size of the current.
The distance from the wire.
exam.tip: Say how: more current is stronger, greater distance is weaker.

exam.q: Current flows into the page through a wire. State the direction of the magnetic field lines around it.
model: Clockwise.
exam.tip: Use the right-hand grip rule with your thumb pointing into the page.

exam.q: Describe the magnetic field inside and outside a current-carrying solenoid.
model: Inside: strong and uniform (parallel, equally spaced lines).
Outside: the same shape as the field of a bar magnet.
exam.tip: Describe both regions.

exam.q: Give three ways of increasing the strength of the magnetic field of a solenoid.
model: Increase the current.
Increase the number of turns.
Add an iron core.
exam.tip: 'Make it bigger' or 'longer' will not score.

exam.q: Explain why soft iron is used for the core of the electromagnet in a scrapyard crane.
model: Soft iron makes the magnetic field much stronger (it becomes an induced magnet).
It loses its magnetism quickly when the current is switched off, so the crane can drop the scrap.
exam.tip: Link the property to the use.

exam.q: Looking at one end of a solenoid, the current flows anticlockwise. Which magnetic pole is at that end? What happens if the current is reversed?
model: North pole.
The poles swap: that end becomes a south pole.
exam.tip: Anticlockwise = N, clockwise = S.

exam.q: Explain why the magnetic field inside a solenoid is stronger than the field around a single straight wire carrying the same current.
model: Each turn of the coil produces its own magnetic field.
Inside the coil the fields from all the turns point in the same direction.
So they add together / reinforce, giving a stronger (uniform) field.
exam.tip: 'Reinforce' or 'add together' is the key idea.

exam.q: Describe an experiment to show that a current in a wire produces a magnetic field, and to find the shape and direction of the field. Include what you would observe.
model: Pass a vertical wire through a horizontal piece of card and connect it to a d.c. supply and switch.
Sprinkle iron filings on the card, switch on and tap the card gently.
The filings form concentric circles around the wire, showing the shape of the field.
Place plotting compasses on the card around the wire: they point along the circles, showing the field direction.
Reverse the current: the compasses point the opposite way round.
Increase the current: the compasses near the wire are deflected more / the pattern extends further; switch off after a short time to stop the wire overheating.
exam.tip: Method, observations for shape and direction, and a safety point.

worked.q: A long straight wire carries current vertically upwards. Using the right-hand grip rule, describe the direction of the field as seen from above, and state what happens to the field at a point 4 cm from the wire if the current is doubled and the point is kept the same.
steps: Point the right thumb upwards along the current.
Looking down from above, the fingers curl anticlockwise.
So the field lines are concentric circles going anticlockwise when viewed from above.
Field strength increases with current, and the distance is unchanged.
Doubling the current doubles the field strength at that point; the direction stays anticlockwise.
worked.ans: Anticlockwise circles viewed from above; the field at 4 cm becomes twice as strong.

worked.q: A student wants to make a stronger electromagnet. She has a coil of 50 turns, a 2 A supply, a steel rod and a soft iron rod. Explain which changes she should make.
steps: More turns give a stronger field, so she should wind more turns onto the same length (for example 100 turns).
A larger current gives a stronger field, so she should increase the current (safely, without overheating the wire).
An iron core makes the field much stronger because it becomes an induced magnet.
She should choose the soft iron rod, not the steel one, because soft iron loses its magnetism when the current is switched off, so the electromagnet can be turned off.
worked.ans: Increase the number of turns, increase the current and use the soft iron rod as a core.

worked.q: Model answer: compare the magnetic field of a solenoid with that of a bar magnet.
steps: Outside the solenoid, the field has the same shape as the field around a bar magnet.
Both have a north pole and a south pole, and the field lines go from N to S outside.
Unlike a bar magnet, the solenoid's field can be switched off and its poles reversed by reversing the current.
Inside the solenoid the field is strong and uniform.
worked.ans: Same shape outside with N and S poles, but the solenoid's field can be switched off, changed in strength and reversed, and is uniform inside.
